canonical_topic: Expected demand vs. worst-case demand as distinct modeling goals
definition: A load forecasting model must be built around its intended use: a utility doing capacity planning may want the heaviest plausible load on a given day (a worst-case forecast) so it can line up enough standby generation, while a trader may instead want the load most likely to actually occur (an expected-value forecast) to support a trading strategy.
core_idea: There is no single 'best' load forecasting model — the right model depends on whether the goal is capacity planning (worst case) or trading (expected/most likely case), and the modeler should reason about the specific goal rather than apply one generic approach.
key_points: Utilities doing capacity planning care about the heaviest plausible load, to ensure sufficient standby generation is available.
Traders care about the load most likely to occur, since it feeds trading decisions.
All forecasting models share similarities, but no model is universally optimal across use cases.
The author frames this as a call for practical judgment: think about the goal and apply common sense rather than a one-size-fits-all technique.
relationships: Applies the general spatial load forecasting concept to two different use cases: utility capacity planning vs. trading
trading_implications: A trader's forecasting model should target the most likely demand outcome, not the worst case a utility would plan around — using the wrong target could bias a trading strategy.
caveats: Assuming one universal load forecast (e.g., a utility's worst-case planning number) is equally appropriate for trading purposes, when the author notes the two use cases call for different modeling targets.
